summary: Describes a preemption priority policy element for signaled admission protocols such as RSVP and COPS.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets an important request bump a less important one when space is limited.

questions: what is the difference between preemption and defending priority
subtitle: A small policy element that ranks flows so important reservations can bump less important ones.

tldr.problem: Capacity-based admission control admits flows in order of arrival until capacity runs out, so an important late flow can be turned away while less important early ones keep their place.
tldr.mechanism: A 12-byte PREEMPTION_PRI policy element carries a preemption priority and a defending priority, plus a merge strategy that tells nodes how to combine priorities when reservations merge.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can preempt lower-priority admitted flows to admit higher-priority ones. This RFC obsoletes RFC 2751 and corrects its RSVP POLICY_DATA P-Type codepoint assignment error.

today: RFC 3181 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2751, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Preemption Priority and Admission Control
sections.content:
Traditional Capacity based Admission Control (CAC) admits new flows until capacity is exhausted, a rule the RFC calls First Come First Admitted. Policy based Admission Control (PAC) tries to reduce the importance of arrival order and uses policy criteria instead. One popular criterion is the rank of a flow relative to others competing for the same node.

Preemption priority only takes effect when the flows trying to get through a node would overbook its resources, so that some would have to be rejected. The priority helps the node choose the most important flows and reject the low-priority ones. Nodes that support preemption should consider priorities to preempt some previously admitted low-priority flows to make room for a newer, high-priority flow.

The document defines the format and applicability of this priority as a policy element carried in the RSVP policy data of RFC 2750, for signaled policy admission protocols such as RSVP and COPS.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the first people in line get the seats. With priorities, a more important person arriving late can take the seat of a less important person, but only when the room is full.

sections.title: Scope and the Usage Model
sections.content:
The policy framework of RFC 2753 describes the parts that take part in policy decisions: the PDP (Policy Decision Point), the PEP (Policy Enforcement Point) and the LDP (Local Decision Point). PREEMPTION_PRI elements are meant to be simple, stateless and light-weight so they can be handled inside a node's LDP.

  • Created by PDPs. A PDP reduces its relevant policy rules into a single priority and passes it downstream to PEPs of the same policy domain that have an LDP but no controlling PDP.
  • Processed by LDPs. An LDP may interpret an element, forward it as is, or merge locally and forward an equivalent merged element. It must follow the merging strategy the PDP encoded.
  • Enforced by PEPs. They work with the node's traffic control module and capacity admission control to enforce priorities and preempt admitted flows when needed.

Because the priority is stateless, needing no past history or outside information to interpret, it is carried in COPS messages as a Stateless Policy Data Decision object.
sections.plainLanguage: A boss writes down a rank, helpers along the way pass the rank on, and the doorkeeper uses it to decide who gets in.

sections.title: The Policy Element Format
sections.content:
A Policy Data object, defined in RFC 2750, may hold one or more policy elements, each representing a different policy. The preemption priority element is 12 bytes long and has these fields: Length (always 12), P-Type (PREEMPTION_PRI = 1), Flags (reserved, always 0), Merge Strategy, Error Code, a reserved byte (always 0), Preemption Priority and Defending Priority.

The two priorities are 16-bit unsigned values, and higher values mean higher priority. The preemption priority is how the new flow ranks against the defending priority of flows already admitted. Once a flow is admitted its preemption priority becomes irrelevant and its defending priority is used instead against new arrivals. A flow's preemption priority must always be less than or equal to its defending priority.

A wide gap between the two adds stability. A moderate preemption priority makes it harder for the flow to preempt others, but once it succeeds the higher defending priority makes it harder for the flow to be preempted. This balances order dependency against priority.
sections.plainLanguage: You have two numbers. One is how strong you are when asking for a seat. The other is how strong you are when someone tries to take your seat, and it is never smaller than the first.

sections.title: Merging Priorities
sections.content:
When two RSVP reservations merge, such as F1 with high QoS and low priority and F2 with low QoS and high priority, the merged reservation has high QoS but an open question: which priority? The RFC names three risks. Free-riders: if the merged flow takes the high priority, F1 gets a priority meant for F2. Denial of service: if it takes the low priority, the flow could be preempted or fail even though F2 asked for high priority. Instability: preemption priority combined with killer reservation and blockade state may cause a reservation to be preempted, reinstated and preempted again periodically.

An LDP computes the merged result in three steps: preemption and defending priority are merged separately; participating elements are selected according to their merge strategy; then the highest priority among the participants is taken.

The three strategies are in the figure below. Strategy 1, taking the priority of the highest QoS, lets an element take part only if its flow contributed to the merged QoS level. It is the recommended strategy and is best at preventing free-riders and denial of service. Strategy 2 lets every element take part; it is not recommended but may be simpler to implement. Strategy 3 allows an element to take part only if all other flows have the same QoS level. It is recommended when reservation homogeneity is coordinated and enforced for the whole multicast tree, and it is more restrictive than strategy 1 but easier to implement.
sections.plainLanguage: When two kids share one seat request, someone has to decide which rank counts. Using the rank of the kid who actually needs the big seat is the fairest way.

sections.title: Modifying Elements and Error Processing
sections.content:
If a POLICY_DATA object is protected by integrity, LDPs should not modify it; they must forward it as is, or its security envelope would be invalid. Otherwise an LDP may merge incoming elements to reduce their size and number. Merging is done separately for each merge strategy, because the RFC knows of no way to merge elements of different strategies without losing information that matters to other nodes. For each strategy the highest value among the participating elements is placed in one outgoing element, so the number of forwarded elements is at most the number of strategies, regardless of the number of receivers.

Errors are sent back as PREEMPTION_PRI error objects. Code 0 is NO_ERROR for regular elements, 1 is PREEMPTION and 2 is HETEROGENEOUS. On preemption, a copy of the preempting flow's element goes back toward the PDP that created the preempted element. That PDP knows both priorities and may build a higher-priority element to try to reinstate the flow. If a flow using the heterogeneous-error strategy meets heterogeneity, its element is sent back toward the receivers with the heterogeneity error code.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers can combine rank notes to save paper, unless the note is sealed. If someone loses their seat, the boss is told who took it, so the boss can write a stronger note.

sections.title: Security, IANA and Status
sections.content:
As with any policy element, the integrity of PREEMPTION_PRI is guaranteed by being encapsulated in a Policy Data object (RFC 2750). The RFC says further security mechanisms are not warranted, because preemption priority gives simple and quick guidance to routers inside a trusted zone, or at least a single zone with no zone boundaries crossed.

For IANA, Standard RSVP Policy Element P-type values are assigned by IETF Consensus action, and P-Type PREEMPTION_PRI is assigned the value 1. The abstract states that this memo corrects an RSVP POLICY_DATA P-Type codepoint assignment error in RFC 2751, which it obsoletes.
sections.plainLanguage: The ranks are only shared among helpers inside one trusted club, so the sealed envelope is enough protection.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Overall length of the element in bytes.

fields.name: Preemption Priority
fields.desc: Priority of the new flow against defending priorities. Higher is more important.

fields.name: Defending Priority
fields.desc: Priority used once the flow is admitted. Never below the preemption priority.

items.label: Highest QoS
items.desc: Take the priority of the highest QoS; recommended.

items.label: Highest priority
items.desc: Take the highest priority; aggressive, not recommended.

items.label: Force error
items.desc: Force an error on a heterogeneous merge.
